title: India to Count Unpaid Work, Gig Workers in Jobs Survey Overhaul
excerpt: The PLFS redesign from January 2027 adds a dedicated sample for digital platform workers and first-time questions on unpaid household and care work, and will change how India's employment numbers read.
body:
• India's statistics ministry has proposed overhauling the Periodic Labour Force Survey from January 2027 to count unpaid household and care work and to capture digital platform workers properly for the first time.
  • A dedicated sampling category will target households with platform workers after the 2026 survey round admitted it captured too few of them; a screening question will ask if any member did platform work in the reference period.
  • New questions for everyone aged 15 and above will cover own-use production, unpaid household and caregiving work, volunteering and unpaid trainee work, enabling annual reporting.
  • For readers, headline unemployment and participation rates from 2027 will not be directly comparable with earlier years — broader counting of work, especially women's unpaid work, will change what the numbers show. Public feedback is open for 15 days.

India has proposed the next overhaul of its main jobs survey, adding unpaid household work to what the country counts and creating a dedicated way to find gig and platform workers, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation said on Friday.

The changes to the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), run by the National Statistics Office since 2017, would take effect from January 2027 when fresh samples are drawn for the 2027-28 cycle, according to Reuters. The ministry has invited comments from policymakers, researchers and the public within 15 days of the 23 October concept note.

Counting the platform workforce properly

The NSO began collecting information on digital platform workers — a subset of gig workers — on an experimental basis in January 2026. "Experience from PLFS 2026 showed that the existing arrangement did not capture an adequate number of digital platform workers," the NSO said in its press note, reported by Upstox.

https://x.com/PIB_India/status/2113539764779663541

The fix is structural. A new Second Stage Stratum based on digital platform work will be added while the existing structure is retained — four strata in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households surveyed in each selected First Stage Unit. A binary screening question, asked in both rural and urban households, will identify whether any member engaged in digital platform work during the reference period, so those households can be sampled deliberately rather than found by chance.

Unpaid work enters the survey

The second change reaches work the PLFS has never measured separately. New questions, asked during the first visit to respondents aged 15 and above in rural and urban areas, will cover own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work and unpaid trainee work, enabling annual reporting, BusinessLine reported.

The concept note states that a substantial proportion of women in India spend considerable time on unpaid household and caregiving activities — cooking, cleaning, childcare and care of elderly, sick or disabled family members — which support other members' paid employment but "have not been measured separately in PLFS until now." The schedule will also test additional questions on labour underutilisation to give a more nuanced picture of slack in the jobs market.

"Half a step."

— K.R. Shyam Sundar, labour economist, on the proposed changes

What changes for the numbers you read

The revisions land amid debate over whether official data reflects underemployment and job quality in the world's most populous country, where headline unemployment stands at 5%, Reuters noted. Labour economist K.R. Shyam Sundar called the changes "half a step," saying many workers operate outside digital platforms, but added that measuring unpaid work could eventually prompt changes in how national income is calculated.

Practically, readers should expect a break in the series. Fresh samples for 2027-28 will use an updated frame reflecting the latest Urban Frame Survey, urbanisation and district boundary changes, with a three-month transition from January 2027 in which monthly estimates are pooled from old and new frames. Broader counting will likely lift measured work participation — particularly for women — without any change in underlying jobs, so year-on-year comparisons across the January 2027 line will need care. The final design follows the 15-day consultation.
